articles.title: Vehicle Report Turns One: Disrupting Used Car Buying for Over 42,000 UAE Drivers and Counting
articles.desc:
A year ago, purchasing a used car in the GCC often meant navigating limited information and a lack of transparency. In response, AutoData Middle East launched Vehicle Report – an AI-powered platform designed to place greater control in the hands of consumers. Over the past 12 months, more than 42,000 users have turned to the service to access verified data on ownership, accident history, valuation, and more. Daily usage has tripled between July 2024 and March 2025, with over 5,000 users now engaging each month. Of those, 84% reported no post-purchase issues, underscoring the platform’s role in reducing buyer risk and building confidence through accurate, accessible insight.

Empowering Informed, Efficient Car Buying

Vehicle Report stands out by turning fragmented automotive data into clear, actionable insight. Built around real consumer needs, the platform supports smarter, safer, and faster decision-making throughout the used car journey, before committing:

Save Money: Compare loan and insurance offers side by side, with market-aligned valuations to avoid overpaying.

Buy Smart: Access a car’s full history, including accidents and ownership lineage, maintenance data, pre-purchase inspection insights and service records, with a single Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) lookup.

Save Time: Instantly aggregating listings, while filtering and forecasting in real-time from multiple sales portals, streamlining the car-buying process.

Through this consolidated approach, the platform is shifting the regional automotive experience from reactive to data-driven, bridging the gap between information and confident decision-making for today’s car buyers.

As the UAE’s used car market continues to grow, residual value performance remains a crucial indicator of vehicle quality and long-term value. In Q2 2025, data from AutoData shows that family-friendly vehicles such as the Kia Carens LX continue to hold strong residual value (78% after 3 years), thanks to a balance of affordability, spacious design, and efficient ownership costs. Within the SUV category, the Toyota Land Cruiser GXR was recognised as the best-value model (81% after 3 years), combining robust specification levels with competitive market pricing and favourable depreciation profiles.

As Vehicle Report continues to gain momentum across the region, AutoData Middle East is expanding its suite of tools to support smarter decisions for both consumers and industry partners.

Among its upcoming innovations is an AI-powered pricing engine that delivers real-time car valuations using over 100 million data points – factoring in market trends, specs, and condition to reveal a vehicle’s true worth, whether buying, selling or trading in.

Also in development is Claim Hub , a tool for insurers to detect total loss vehicles, reduce fraud, and accelerate claims – enhancing accountability across the ecosystem and building long-term trust for buyers.

With a future-ready focus, AutoData is bridging data and trust to make car ownership safer, simpler, and smarter.

“Our mission has always been to bring clarity and confidence to the automotive ecosystem,” said Sebastian Fuchs, Managing Director of AutoData Middle East. “With advanced AI at its core, Vehicle Report delivers real-time, market-specific pricing and risk analysis – helping buyers save up to 25% on average. More than a history check, it’s a decision-making engine that unifies pricing, ownership, and insurance data to transform how used cars are bought and sold. As we grow, we’re focused on deeper integrations with insurers, banks, and marketplaces, and on launching tools like AutoMagic and Claim Hub to further streamline the process. We’re proud to be raising the bar for transparency and intelligence in automotive transactions.”

With AI-powered technology, trust, and transparency at its core, Vehicle Report is redefining how the UAE buys and sells used cars. Now entering its second year, it’s more than just a report – it’s a smart ecosystem built to empower better decisions, from valuation to insurance to ownership.

Learn more about Vehicle Report – AutoData Middle East’s AI-powered platform helping over 42,000 users make smarter car decisions: www.vehiclereport.me

Software is increasingly shaping vehicle functions, while at the same time more and more data is being generated and used for new applications. This transformation opens up new possibilities for connected vehicles and services, but also presents vehicle manufacturers with growing technical and regulatory challenges. Knorr-Bremse is actively shaping this transformation and will demonstrate at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover (September 15–20, 2026, Hall 12, Booth C21) how the vehicle network is evolving into a seamless digital ecosystem—from vehicle architecture to the trailer and into the aftermarket.

Bernd Spies, Member of the Executive Board of Knorr-Bremse AG and responsible for the Commercial Vehicle Systems Division: “The future of commercial vehicles is software-driven and connected. This development opens up new opportunities for all market participants. That is why we are consistently evolving our offering from individual products toward integrated digital service and system solutions. For OEMs, we are focusing on open, manufacturer-independent platforms. At the same time, with the CVS Service Platform, we are systematically expanding our digital offerings for vehicle operations and the aftermarket.”

The CVS Service Platform brings together Knorr-Bremse’s digital solutions for OEMs, fleets, and workshops. It integrates software, diagnostics, and service into a fully digital system for connected vehicles and services. In this way, the platform helps simplify operational and service processes and make them more efficient. Both OEM solutions and digital applications for the aftermarket are built on this platform.

As the proportion of software in vehicles increases, the demands on cybersecurity, updates, and compliance rise significantly. Regulations such as UN ECE R155 on cybersecurity and UN ECE R156 for software updates require end-to-end digital processes to manage software versions securely and transparently. Knorr-Bremse supports OEMs with an ISO 24089-certified Software Update Management System (SUMS), which is integrated into the cloud-based Online Configuration Tool (OCT) and is already in series production. Software and configuration versions can be managed in a structured manner, updates can be rolled out automatically, and processes from production to the aftermarket can be digitally mapped. This results in stable, efficient workflows within an end-to-end process chain. These workflows help OEMs reduce operating costs, simplify processes, and efficiently comply with regulatory requirements.

Knorr-Bremse has already established this architecture in the trailer sector: The electronic trailer braking system iTEBS® X combines braking functions, sensors, and control in a scalable system architecture. Additionally, other trailer systems are fully integrated into SUMS—including brake control systems such as iTEPM (Intelligent Trailer Electro-Pneumatic Module) and TRM (Trailer Roadtrain Module), the iXPAND (Intelligent Electronic Port Expander) expansion interface, as well as tire pressure monitoring systems such as iTPMS (Intelligent Tire Pressure Monitoring System) and third-party systems. Diagnostic, update, and software processes are thereby transformed into integrated digital workflows. In this way, Knorr-Bremse lays the groundwork for future E/E architectures, over-the-air updates, and automated functions within vehicle networks.

In addition, Knorr-Bremse is working with partners to expand its offering to include open platforms such as the Cojali Digital Hub. This manufacturer-independent platform enables OEMs to consolidate various software applications into a centralized, cyber-secure environment. Software update packages can thus be managed centrally, from production through to the aftermarket. With WESP CV , Knorr-Bremse has expanded the CVS Service Platform to include a data-driven analytics and benchmarking application for commercial vehicle workshops. Based on performance indicators, workshops can compare their processes with those of other businesses and systematically identify optimization potential. This creates transparency around their own performance and helps workshops continuously improve productivity, capacity utilization and profitability.

Knorr-Bremse (ISIN: DE000KBX1006, ticker symbol: KBX) is the global market and technology leader for braking systems and a leading supplier of other innovative solutions for the rail and commercial vehicle industries. Knorr-Bremse’s products make a decisive contribution to greater safety and energy efficiency on rail tracks and roads around the world. About 30,000 employees at over 100 locations in 30 countries develop and produce innovative solutions and services that meet the highest technological standards. In 2025, Knorr-Bremse’s two divisions together generated revenues of approximately € 7.8 billion. articles.title: Books from two industry veterans: one to draw kids to skilled trades, another to offer claims guidance
articles.desc:
Two longtime collision repairers have written books they hope will help the industry and consumers, with one seeking to show children a full range of career options in the skilled trades.

Jaime Shewbridge, a welding and automotive instructor with a 30-plus-year career, said she discovered fourth grade is the ideal time to start talking to kids about the careers that are out there. She believes targeting high school students is waiting until it’s too late because by then, most have already chosen the career they want to pursue.

“There’s so much more than just going to school to get a four-year degree; they don’t really tell kids that,” Shewbridge said. “When they do, it’s late middle school, early high school, and a lot of times they’ve already made up their mind, or they’ve had the adults in their life kind of funnel them towards college… It’s not for everybody. We have to do a better job explaining to kids: if it’s not for you and you love taking model airplanes apart, then maybe you would like to be an airplane mechanic, and we need those.”

That’s just one example career she plans to cover in a book series. She said each role she writes about will be based on real-life experience from professionals she knows.

Shewbridge said she hopes her books will address two stigmas: “white collar” jobs are better than “blue collar” jobs, and that the skilled trades are just for boys.

The first book, “Levi Doesn’t Know,” is written from the perspective of 9-year-old Levi, who is often asked by adults: “What do you want to be when you grow up?”

Shewbridge said, unfortunately, adults her age, and possibly the generation after her, “still believe that being in a shop or any type of blue-collar trade is dirty and ‘less than’ somehow.”

“It’s not,” she said. “These technicians are incredible. They do things we could never do… I have a college degree; I’m not discounting it. It’s very useful and necessary for a lot of jobs, but it’s not the only way. It’s not the only door there is. There’s trade schools, there’s on-the-job training, there’s the military.”

She added that the “blue collar” versus “white collar” stigma causes many technicians to lose confidence in their skills.

“I have a lot of them that will tell me when I hand them paperwork, ‘I’m doing this because I didn’t do well in school and you’re handing me a bunch of paperwork to read,'” Shewbridge said. “They always discount how smart they are; they discount their own ability, and they act like they’re a body man because they couldn’t do anything else. It’s so not true. They’re some of the smartest people you’ll ever meet.

“One thing I don’t think the public realizes is they literally have your life in their hands. If they don’t fix that car right, you might not live the next time… It really comes down to their talent, skill, and ability, whether your car wrecks the next time correctly or not.”

“Levi Doesn’t Know” covers what it’s like to work as a welder, her own career.

“My favorite part of the first book is when Levi comes home from school, and he’s disheartened that he didn’t know what he wanted to be, but all of his friends knew,” Shewbridge said. “He walked into the garage, and he was talking to his grandmother and, at some point, realizes that she’s a welding teacher. And his first thing was, ‘But you’re a girl.’ And even in the fourth grade, there’s still that perception of boy jobs and girl jobs from watching TV and maybe seeing a certain job done by a certain demographic.”

Shewbridge said, looking back to when she was a fourth grader, she wouldn’t have thought then she would become a welding teacher.

“I would’ve never said that was true; never, ever,” she said. “That was the farthest thing from my mind that could have been. To know that I am one, I am female, and there aren’t that many of us, I think that ‘aha’ moment for Levi will also bring that same moment for kids in the class that reads it to say, ‘Well, I am a girl, but I could also be a welding instructor, or I could be a welder, or I could be a body tech, or I could be an airplane mechanic, or whatever. Just because I’m X, Y, and Z doesn’t define what job I can have.’ I think women in the skilled trades still face that stigma even as adults. Most of the time, I’m the only female in the room.”

Another book in the series will cover several body shop careers. Shewbridge said the goal of that book is to show kids that if, for example, they start as a body technician or painter and want to transition into another role, they don’t have to start over.

“You could be a manager, you could be a production manager, you could be a parts person, you could own a shop,” she said. “There’s so many more jobs just within each skilled trade… I think we’re doing a disservice to a lot of kids that would thrive in a job with their hands that are never given the opportunity to even know that it’s out there.”

Shewbridge said she also hopes kids will talk to their parents about what they learn from her books

articles.title: Federal Reserve senior policy advisor: Collision shops at front lines of auto industry changes
articles.desc:
As the U.S. auto industry faces multiple disruptions, collision repairers are on the front lines of observing how consumers respond to changes in a sector critical to the nation’s gross domestic product (GDP), Kristen Dziczek, senior policy advisor at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said during The Industry Exchange at the Collision Industry Conference in Las Vegas.

“I think your shop is really where this broad economy meets people’s pocketbooks,” Dziczek said. “You’re seeing that decision made right on the front lines.”

Dziczek says those collision shop experiences will tell a story about the economy before data shows it.

“You’re seeing how trade increases the price of the part shipping,” Dziczek said. “You’re seeing how technology changes the things you have to do for calibration and the arguments you have to have about paying for those sorts of things. You’re seeing how finances change to higher deductibles; how the loss per mile is lower, but the loss per collision is higher.”

Part of Dziczek’s job is to have conversations with those throughout the auto industry, including collision repair businesses, about what they are seeing in the economy, she said.

“There’s a bunch of really smart people who are doing very complicated mathematical models of the economy, and we listen to all of that, and then they say, ‘And now, what’s really going on in the economy?’” she said.

Dziczek has been working at the Federal Reserve for about five years. Previously, she worked at General Motors, the UAW, in various auto industry roles for Congress, and at a nonprofit auto industry think tank.

“I think I have the coolest job in the auto industry,” she added.

Auto makes up about 5% of the U.S. GDP and employs more than 1 million people, Dziczek explained. She added that the industry touches all the “big moving parts,” like steel, aluminum, copper, microchips, oil, critical minerals, and magnets.

“We’ve got lenders, we’ve got insurers, we’ve got repair, we’ve got customers,” Dziczek said. “We’re [Federal Reserve] looking at consumer behavior, we’re looking at banking behavior, we’re looking at all sorts of things through the lens of the auto industry. It’s super duper important, and there are very few other segments of the economy that are 5% of the GDP.”

During the Industry Exchange, Aaron Schulenburg, executive director of the Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS), asked Dziczek about the current and possible future pressures on the auto industry.

In 2026, gas prices, vehicle sales, tariffs, EVs, and technologies were some of the developments that the Federal Reserve paid attention to, she said.

“I’ll say this isn’t the highest gas prices have ever been, but it is the highest they’ve ever been this time of year,” Dziczek said as she ran through the list. “Sales have been remarkably resilient, coming in around $16 million this year. Consumers keep buying, so there’s been not really any kind of pullback with that. We’ve seen a few little blips from supply chain disruptions here and there, and then of course tariffs and how tariffs have played out.”

When discussing consumer spending, she said buyers seem to “be fine.” However, she added that new car buyers tend to make six-figure incomes. She added that there are some troubling signs with auto delinquencies, adding that they are at the highest level since 2010.

Dziczek said the EV reset has shifted focus to hybrids. Currently, about 16.7% of the vehicle market is hybrid, and some vehicles only have a hybrid configuration.

Electrified vehicles overall are about 24% of the market.

“That EV reset, however, burned about $100 billion in capital for the automakers,” Dziczek said. “A huge, huge turnaround, while the rest of the world continues on in electrification.”

Schulenburg asked if there are other vehicle technologies that the Federal Reserve is watching.

In response, Dziczek said two technologies that are most important to the collision repair industry: manufacturing changes to fewer parts and ADAS/automation.

Automakers are following Tesla’s lead on gigacasting to make vehicles less expensive, she said.

This year, Ford has been at the forefront of the conversation about gigacasting (or megacasting as Ford refers to it).

The automaker announced it would invest $5 billion to change how it makes electric vehicles to lower its EV prices. The target starting price for a mid-sized EV truck is $30,000 compared to the average EV cost of $56,000, according to CBS News .

The shift includes changing how the assembly line operates and a reduction in the total number of parts used in the vehicle. For example, a Ford press release says the wiring harness will be 4,000 feet shorter.

Dziczek said replacing many parts with fewer parts does make vehicles easier to manufacture but “maybe not easier to repair.”

It also could have implications for the companies that make the parts being reduced by the automakers.

ADAS and automation are changing the industry

This year’s MSO Symposium brought together “the Four Aces” — the CEOs of Boyd Group, Caliber, Classic Collision, and Crash Champions —in Las Vegas on Monday, who ultimately landed on a simple conclusion: the collision repair industry depends on the right people fitting into the right roles.

When moderator Dan Risley asked what they’re hearing from investors and other stakeholders about the industry today, Boyd Group CEO Brian Kaner responded that the industry isn’t “recession-proof, but it is recession-resilient.”

“There are plenty of opportunities for us to continue to grow our businesses,” he said. “It all comes down to making sure you have the right people in the right roles with the right capabilities. However, in response to a different question Risley posed about the “temperature” of each MSO’s team leaders, Crash Champions CEO Matt Ebert and Kaner agreed it’s a tense, stressful time for them, and made some important points about estimators.

Ebert added that general managers also face pressure to keep customers, employees, and insurance companies happy while trying to make money and handle the safety, legal, and logistical pieces of their jobs.

There’s not enough of them. There’s not enough of them that understand the metrics. Brad Anderson, who joined the collision repair industry in June to take over as CEO of Classic Collision, said he believes all jobs in the industry are hard.

articles.title: TechForce CEO warns collision industry risks being left behind in skilled trades workforce push
articles.desc:
The pendulum is swinging, and major corporations with deep pockets are discussing the skilled workforce shortage, but that also means competition for a seat at the table will intensify, Jennifer Maher, TechForce Foundation CEO, told Repairer Driven News.

​“I worry that I don’t hear that same momentum in the collision industry,” Maher said.

​The U.S.Bureau of Labor has identified 47 different technician jobs using its standard occupational classification (SOC) system, Maher said. She said this includes everything from wind turbine techs to elevator technicians.

​“We’re all competing for the same person,” Maher said. “The person who is curious, likes to problem solve, takes it apart and puts it back together, gets a thrill out of making things work.”

​The collision industry competes with all of these different technician sectors, she said. The industry is also competing with all of the skilled trades, which include electricians, construction workers and plumbers.

​“You can’t just look at how to build collision techs in the collision program,” Maher said. “You have to cast your net really wide. We’re competing with all of those sectors.”

​“I call them our hidden heroes because we all need technicians and we need to recognize and start talking about the importance of those service and maintenance technicians,” Maher said.

​As the pendulum swings, the conversation is heavily focused on construction jobs.

“I appreciate the need to bring back manufacturing and build more plants, build more housing, and build more data centers. That’s exciting and great, but in my world, I’m asking how do we keep what we have moving?”

​If technicians get lost in the conversation, then people will find themselves waiting on the tarmac because of a shortage of airplane technicians or waiting two months for their vehicle to be repaired because of a shortage of auto technicians, she said.

​“Techs are important and we need to be at the table,” Maher said. “That’s the bottom line, technicians need to be in the headlines and they need to be part of the excitement around the skilled trades.”

​The top 10 technician fields identified by the U.S. Bureau of Labor adds up to a workforce of 7 million people, she said.

​“Collectively they are a huge force but they are buried, hidden and not talked about,” Maher said.

​Even under the Bureau of Labor’s classification system, technicians are scattered throughout different industries including transportation, energy, industrial manufacturing and construction, she added.

articles.title: Volkswagen-Electronic-Parking-Brake
articles.desc:
The majority of Volkswagen vehicles sold in the past decade have electronic parking brakes. However, most customers don’t even realize that the vehicle has an electronic parking brake, because the system engages and disengages the parking brake automatically on most vehicles. But, when the system fails and turns on the light or has a warning in the driver information center, then the customer will notice.

- Porsche TPMS: The First Carmaker To The Game

If you are doing a brake job on a vehicle with an electronic parking brake, you will need a scan tool with the proper software for the parking brake system to retract the calipers, adjust and perform diagnostics. There are no shortcuts on YouTube. You can find videos that involve removing the electric motor, jumping connectors and disassembling the parking brake mechanism. But, these methods are very risky and can damage the vehicle and kill productivity. Unapproved methods will set malfunction codes, and the worst-case scenario is that you could damage the unit.

The VW system that was installed on many of its platforms starting in 2004 is an example of a system that requires a scan tool to replace the rear brake pads.

The system has stepper motors on the back of the caliper that actuate the piston. The motor can be removed from the caliper, though the ignition should be switched off for at least 30 seconds before removing the connector.

The motor is sealed to the caliper with an o-ring around the spindle. The condition of this o-ring is critical for the life of the motor and should be lightly lubricated with brake fluid. If the o-ring fails, water and debris will be one step closer to the motor gears.

The spindle on the caliper can be rocked slightly with a torx bit so the motor seats in the spindle. Don’t force the motor assembly onto the caliper, because damage to the housing can occur.

On recent platforms, VW have outfitted the motors with a sensor that can measure brake pad wear and adjust the pads for the least amount of drag. During this adjustment on some vehicles, the pad thickness is calculated. The system counts the number of rotations of the motor with a hall effect sensor inside the unit.

Inspecting the caliper, hardware and motors may not give you a complete picture of what is happening with these systems. Having access to a scan tool can reduce diagnostic time.

The OEMs have built-in bi-directional protocols to retract the parking brake so the pads can be replaced. A dedicated brake tool or enhanced scan tool is able to command these protocols and interrogate the module for codes and faults.

The Electronic Parking Brake Module (EPBM) is the module on the CAN bus of most vehicles equipped with this system. Any missing data for vehicle speed, gear position or brake pedal input will cause a problem with the system.

Some systems use information from the electric parking brake to track shoe and pad wear. The system will count the number of turns the actuator makes or the position of the stepper motor to determine the thickness of the friction material.

If you do find yourself working on a vehicle whose electronic parking brake will not disengage, the first thing to do is look at the basics. Some systems require that the doors be shut and the brake pedal depressed. Some models may even require the seat belt to be buckled. Simple items like a defective brake pedal or door switch may hinder operation. Also, in some cases, the button may be defective. On some vehicles, the operation of the switch can be verified with a scan tool.

articles.desc:
Despite its age, the 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is a popular car you may very well see come through the shop —especially those on the tail end of that year range. Let’s go over the step-by-step brake job process.

The 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is based on the Ford global C1 platform, shared with the European Ford Focus and Volvo S40. Nothing is really groundbreaking about the mechanical brake system, but not paying attention to the details can end in a post-brake-job comeback.

A key service issue concerns the hydraulics and ABS system. The older the car, the greater the chance the brake fluid has not been serviced. Over time this can cause issues with the ABS hydraulic control unit.

For almost 10 years, Mazda used the same caliper, pad and rotor design. Pads should be replaced when there is 2mm or less of friction material. If the rotors are any thicker, they have enough material on them to last at least one turning on the lathe. The runout specification for these vehicles is .002” and disc thickness variation should be far below .0005”.

Mazda claims repeated panic braking may raise the temperature in some portions of the disc plate by approx. 1,000°C (l,832°F). This temperature is almost near impossible to achieve this side of a high-speed police chase.

The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 75 ft./lbs.

All Mazda3 models have rear disc brakes. The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 55 ft./lbs.

Mazda uses a hand brake that is incorporated into the rear caliper, and a couple of systems are employed to retract rear pistons. The later-model cars require the familiar method of turning the piston clockwise while applying pressure, where others will have a plug on the back side of the caliper that provides access for an Allen wrench to facilitate retracting the piston. Be careful as you retract the piston.

After the pads are replaced, pump the pedal and adjust the parking brake mechanism in the rear calipers. If the level has too much travel, perform the following steps:

Remove the service hole cover of the rear console.

Turn the adjusting nut and adjust the parking brake lever.

After adjustment, pull the parking brake lever one notch and verify that the parking brake warning light illuminates and the rear brakes do not drag.

The Mazda3 comes in two styles, ABS and ABS with Dynamic Stability Control (DSC). Both systems connect to other vehicle components via a high-speed serial data bus. The DSC system ties more components together (like a yaw/pitch sensor and steering position sensor) onto the bus.

If you are seeing communication-related DTCs, it is essential that you fully diagnose problems with the system before you start replacing sensors and modules. Some of these vehicles have been on the road for more than six years and the connections will be starting to corrode and fret.

One of the main facilitators of ABS/DCS problems are the connectors, especially under the hood where the control/modulator unit connects. Being able to measure values at the connectors and observe data on a scan tool is essential for diagnosing problems.

The biggest ABS issue with the three generations of Mazda 3 is power. With some higher mileage vehicles, the battery cables, wiring from the power distribution box or the ground connection (behind the driver’s side headlight at G02) can have enough resistance so the voltage drops below 8 volts. When this happens, the ABS module cuts control and the electronic brake distribution system is disabled.

If a modulator/control unit is replaced, the pressure sensors must be recalibrated with a scan tool that is able to communicate with the chassis/ABS module. If this is not performed, it can result in brake failure and lock up.

If you have DTCs C1141, C1142, C1143, C1144, C1233, C1234, C1235 or C1236 (ABS wheel-speed sensor/ABS sensor rotor), chances are something is wrong with the wheel bearings. Another cause for these codes could be an accumulation of metal debris on the sensor. The front bearings are press-in cartridge-style units. Rear wheel bearings are hub units. In the front, the tone ring, or encoder, is on the inner seal of the bearing and the sensor is mounted in the knuckle. The parameters for these codes to be set include abnormalities in the signal such as a weak signal or large differences in the value when compared to the other sensors.

articles.title: Litens Aftermarket’s Scott Howat on An Engineering-Driven Approach
articles.desc:
This episode of DriveTime features Scott Howat, director of sales and marketing, Litens Aftermarket N.A.

- AutoZone’s Phil Daniele on ‘Putting Customers First’

Howat said the company’s engineering-driven approach is what differentiates its belt drive tensioners. With a history of innovation dating back to its founder’s invention of the first belt tensioner in 1979, Litens has developed an extensive portfolio of patented technologies. articles.title: The Downside of Regenerative Braking
articles.desc:
Regenerative braking allows electric vehicles to recover energy during deceleration. Instead of converting all vehicle momentum into heat at the brake rotors, the electric motor acts as a generator. This slows the vehicle while returning some energy to the battery.

- AutoZone’s Phil Daniele on ‘Putting Customers First’

- Niterra President and CEO Mike Schwab on ‘Delivering Trusted Solutions’

The process can significantly reduce the use of conventional friction brakes. However, reduced brake usage can also create maintenance challenges involving corrosion and component operation.

On conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, brake pads regularly contact the rotors during braking. This friction helps remove light surface corrosion from the rotor faces.

EVs with aggressive regenerative braking may use their friction brakes less frequently. Exposure to moisture, road salt and humidity can then allow corrosion to develop on the rotor surfaces.

EV Regenerative Braking and Rotor Corrosion

Light surface rust is not necessarily a problem because normal brake applications can remove it. However, corrosion can progress when friction brakes are not used regularly.

Over time, heavier rust, pitting and scaling can develop on the rotors. Once the rotor surfaces deteriorate significantly, normal brake applications may not restore their condition.

Reduced friction brake usage can also extend brake pad life. However, brake components can develop problems unrelated to friction material wear.

Corrosion may form around brake pad hardware, caliper brackets, slide pins and other components. Pads can become restricted in their brackets, while caliper components may develop problems from limited movement.

As a result, brake components may require replacement because of corrosion or restricted movement rather than normal wear.

How Regenerative and Friction Braking Work Together

Electric vehicles still require conventional hydraulic friction brakes to maintain stopping performance.

Regenerative braking may become reduced or unavailable under certain operating conditions. These include a fully charged battery, very cold battery temperatures, vehicle stability control intervention or certain system faults.

EV braking systems blend regenerative braking with conventional hydraulic friction braking to provide the stopping performance drivers expect.

This makes conventional brake system condition an important consideration, even when regenerative braking reduces normal friction brake usage.

EV Brake Inspection and Maintenance Considerations

Technicians should account for reduced friction brake usage when inspecting electric vehicle braking systems.

Measuring brake pad thickness alone may not provide a complete picture of component condition.

EV regenerative braking improves efficiency by recovering energy and can substantially extend brake pad life. However, reduced friction brake usage can also increase the potential for corrosion and restricted component movement.

Brake condition assessments should account for both friction material wear and the effects of limited brake usage.

articles.title: Brake Job: 2020–2026 Buick Encore GX
articles.desc:
I was recently working on an ASE A5 test-prep article, and we reached the section on parking brakes. Most parking brakes act on the rear wheels, so the test is structured around that arrangement. But some vehicles have parking brakes on the front wheels. I knew that some older Saabs and Datsuns used front-wheel parking brakes. One modern example is the Buick Encore GX.

- Alignment Specs: 2021–Current Ford Mustang Mach-E

On these models, pulling the park-brake switch sends a signal to the Electronic Brake Control Module. The module supplies 12 volts to the apply-control circuits and ground to the release-control circuits, activating the left and right park-brake actuators and applying the brakes.

Pressing the switch sends a signal to the module to release the brakes. The module supplies 12 volts to the release-control circuits and ground to the apply-control circuits, activating the actuators and releasing the brakes. Depending on the vehicle, the switch may be a push-button style. Pressing it commands the parking brakes to apply or release based on their current position.

The parking brake will release automatically if the engine is running, the vehicle is shifted into gear, and the driver attempts to move off. Avoid rapid acceleration while the parking brake is applied to help preserve the parking-brake lining.

The Electronic Brake Control Module, also called the Brake System Control Module, controls the park-brake motor circuits and runs diagnostics to verify that they are operating properly.

To replace the brake pads, the park-brake caliper pistons must be fully retracted. There are two ways to put the parking brake into service mode. The preferred method is to use a scan tool with a service-mode function. If you do not have a compatible scan tool, use this procedure:

Turn the ignition on with the engine off.

Press the accelerator pedal halfway down.

Move the park-brake switch to the release position and hold it for 10 seconds. Release the switch.

Within five seconds, move the switch to the release position again.

The actuator bolts to the back of the caliper and is not included with a replacement caliper. If you remove the actuator, GM recommends replacing the caliper’s O-ring. Front-wheel parking brakes may be a novelty, but they make an interesting piece of trivia to test your technician friends on.

articles.title: What Tire Wear Reveals About Suspension and Alignments
articles.desc:
A driver rolls into the shop complaining that their tires are wearing out faster than expected. The vehicle drives reasonably well, and there are no obvious suspension noises. But a closer look at the tread tells a different story.

- Reading Brake Pad and Rotor Wear: A Diagnostic Guide

Uneven tire wear can reveal problems with alignment, suspension components, tire inflation and ride control. Learning how to recognize these patterns gives technicians a valuable diagnostic advantage.

The key is understanding what each wear pattern means and knowing which components to inspect next.

Start With Tire Pressure and Tread Depth

Before recommending an alignment or replacing suspension components, check the basics.

Inspect all four tires. Measure and record tread depth across the inner, center and outer portions of each tire. Compare the readings to identify differences in wear.

Next, check inflation pressure against the vehicle manufacturer’s specifications. Underinflation often increases wear along both shoulders, while sustained overinflation can increase center tread wear.

Don’t overlook the tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS). A warning light, damaged sensor or incorrect pressure setting may contribute to a problem that has gone unnoticed.

Also look for mismatched tires, damaged wheels and evidence of missed tire rotations.

These initial checks help determine whether the cause is tire maintenance, vehicle geometry or a mechanical problem.

Inner-Edge Wear: Check Camber, Toe and Ride Height

When the inside shoulder wears faster than the rest of the tread, alignment geometry should be one of the first areas to investigate.

Negative camber means the top of the wheel tilts inward relative to the vehicle. Excessive negative camber can place additional load on the inner shoulder.

Toe settings also matter. When wheels point too far inward or outward relative to the vehicle’s direction of travel, the tires scrub against the road instead of rolling cleanly.

Independent rear suspensions deserve particular attention. Worn bushings can change wheel geometry during acceleration, braking and cornering.

Shop tip: Measure ride height before performing an alignment. If the suspension is sitting below specification, adjusting alignment angles alone may not solve the problem.

Outer-Edge Wear: Inspect Alignment and Body Control

Excessive wear on the outside shoulder may indicate an alignment problem or excessive loading during cornering.

Positive camber, incorrect toe settings and worn suspension components can contribute to outer-edge wear.

Consider how the vehicle is driven. Crossovers and SUVs have relatively high centers of gravity, which can increase weight transfer during turns.

When springs, shocks or struts no longer control suspension movement effectively, the tire may experience additional loading and irregular wear.

Diagnostic reminder: Outer-edge wear does not automatically mean the shocks are bad. Verify alignment and mechanical condition before recommending replacement parts.

Feathering occurs when the tread blocks develop a sharp edge on one side and a smoother, rounded edge on the other.

You may not notice feathering immediately during a visual inspection. Carefully running your hand across the tread in opposite directions can help identify the pattern.

Feathering commonly indicates an incorrect toe setting.

However, toe can change when worn steering or suspension components move under load. That means the alignment readings may not tell the entire story.

Check for looseness in tie rods, control arm bushings and other steering components before making adjustments.

Remember that changing camber or caster can affect toe. That’s why toe is normally adjusted after other applicable alignment angles.

Cupping and Scalloping: Look Beyond Alignment

Cupping creates irregular high and low spots around the tire’s circumference. The pattern may resemble a series of shallow dips in the tread.

Shocks and struts help control wheel movement as the vehicle travels over bumps. If they lose damping ability, the tire may move excessively and develop irregular wear.

However, wheel imbalance can create similar symptoms.

A vehicle’s suspension geometry is designed around a specified operating height.

When springs weaken or suspension components wear, ride height can change. That affects camber, toe and the position of suspension control arms.

A small height difference may have a meaningful impact on tire wear.

articles.title: Investing in the Vehicles the Aftermarket Will Be Repairing
articles.desc:
Preparing for the next generation of vehicles takes money and so does keeping up with the ones already in the shop. When you consider investments for 2027, both of those aspects deserve attention. The challenge is deciding how much to commit to each as repair needs develop at different speeds.

- AI Can Do the Math. Humans Still Make the Magic.

- AI & the Aftermarket: NTN Bearing Corporation of America’s Charles Harris

- Are We Asking the Wrong Questions About AI?

The headlines that flooded AftermarketNews website in the past month offer a useful view of that balancing act. Suppliers are developing products for electric drive units while expanding conventional transmission coverage. They are advancing familiar battery technology and redesigning components around problems that emerge after years of use. The opportunities span vehicles of different ages and technologies, all competing for a place in the business plan.

The latest powertrain forecast from the Auto Care Association and MEMA Aftermarket Suppliers helps explain why such planning requires patience. Developed with Strategy&, PwC’s strategy division, the report projects hybrids will account for 32% of U.S. new-vehicle sales in 2035, up from 17% in 2026. It also expects the number of hybrid models to triple between 2025 and 2035.

“Hybrids are becoming a bigger part of the picture, and suppliers need to plan for that reality,” said Philip Atkins, director of strategic research and planning at MEMA Aftermarket Suppliers. “The mix of vehicles on the road will keep changing, and understanding where that demand is headed will help companies make better decisions about products and investment.”

Those are new-vehicle sales projections. Their implications for independent repair develop over time, as vehicles age and their service requirements become clearer. Some of that change is happening within categories the aftermarket already knows well.

Clarios’ expansion of its hAGM battery technology, for example, addresses growing demands on low-voltage electrical systems across powertrain types. More electronics, connectivity and energy-management functions place additional demands on the 12-volt battery, including when the vehicle is parked. The company is applying the technology to future original-equipment programs and, through its OPTIMA REDTOP with hAGM+ technology, the premium replacement market.

“The technology trends shaping future vehicles will also shape the replacement market,” said Marc Andraca, president of U.S. and Canada region at Clarios.

So even a well-established replacement category can require continued development as the systems around it change. Familiarity with the product does not settle the question of what customers will need from its next generation.

Schaeffler’s recent portfolio announcements show how several investment horizons can sit alongside one another. The company is expanding electronics capabilities through its integration of Vitesco Technologies and adding conventional transmission coverage, including an 8L90 torque converter. Its E-Axle RepSystem 2 in1 bearing repair kit enables targeted repairs within electric drive units as an alternative to replacing larger assemblies.

Each addresses a particular repair need, but taken together, they illustrate the breadth of development work that a more varied vehicle population can require. The investment extends into what information and technical support do customers need to use those products?

Dorman’s new aluminum oil filter housing brings the discussion back to an existing application. Designed for select Genesis, Hyundai and Kia vehicles, it addresses an original equipment plastic housing that the company said can degrade, warp or crack after prolonged exposure to heat and chemicals. Dorman’s replacement uses high-pressure die-cast aluminum to address that weakness.

For leaders weighing next year’s commitments, these stories suggest that the timing of investment deserves as much scrutiny as its direction. Vehicle populations, emerging failure points and customer experience can help test whether an opportunity is becoming ready for the business to serve.

The vehicles that will shape the aftermarket’s next decade are entering service alongside those that still have years of repairs ahead. Preparing for that future means staying close enough to customers to recognize what is arriving in their bays, then putting the right resources behind it.

The Schaeffler division is making two Vitesco repair solutions available to the automotive aftermarket: a Voltage Stabilization System (VSS) for micro hybrid vehicles from Toyota and Peugeot S.A. (PSA), and a 48V DC/DC converter for Ford mild hybrid vehicles.

- Preventing EV Lithium-ion Battery Fires

- Charging and Replacing Batteries with Advanced Power Management Systems

The VSS is available immediately. According to Schaeffler, it prevents voltage drops that can occur during automatic start-stop operation in micro-hybrid vehicles. The system consists of an Energy Storage System (ESS) with high-performance capacitors and a Power Electronics Unit (PEU).

Schaeffler notes that during the engine start process, the capacitors release energy stored while driving within a very short time, compensating for the high-power demand. Starting the engine via a starter-generator requires a comparatively high amount of energy.

If this energy is drawn solely from the conventional 12-volt electrical system, the voltage can briefly drop by several volts, causing visible flickering of the vehicle’s lighting and electronic displays. Schaeffler said that by stabilizing the voltage supply, the capacitors ensure smooth engine restarting and contribute to longer battery life, improved driving comfort and compliance with current emissions standards.

The Schaeffler Vitesco 48V DC/DC converter, available in May, is used in mild-hybrid vehicles equipped with a 48V starter generator and an additional battery to enable more efficient power delivery and boost performance during acceleration, the company says. The converter links the vehicle’s 48-volt electrical system with the 12-volt onboard electronics.

The converter is a component of energy management in mild-hybrid vehicles and for achieving type-approval compliant CO2 emissions. Its bidirectional design allows 12-volt components to be supplied from the 48-volt network while charging the starter battery. Conversely, in the event of a temporary failure, the 48-volt system can also draw energy from the 12-volt network, the company notes.

articles.title: 21.10.2026 Press release Venture Capital Bosch Ventures invests in Sonexos Stuttgart, Germany / Lausanne, Switzerland – Bosch Ventures is investing in Swiss deep-tech company Sonexos as part of its CHF 5 million Pre-Series A financing round. The round will support the industrialization and market introduction of Sonexos’ novel plasma-based technology for active noise control.Sonexos is developing a new way to tackle one of acoustics’ persistent engineering challenges: low-frequency noise from fans, compressors and motors. Conventional solutions typically require significant space and material and can restrict airflow. Sonexos instead uses an electronically controlled layer of plasma to absorb sound, creating a thin, lightweight solution with no moving parts.Deep tech with industrial relevance and societal impactFor Bosch Ventures, Sonexos brings together differentiated deep technology, industrial relevance and the potential to improve everyday life, a strong expression of Bosch’s “Invented for life” principle.“Technology is most valuable when it moves out of the laboratory and solves problems people experience every day. Sonexos is a strong example of that principle: outstanding deep tech addressing a very tangible challenge, with applications ranging from the appliances in our homes to the infrastructure powering the digital economy,” says Dr. Ingo Ramesohl, Managing Director of Bosch Ventures. “What convinced us in particular is the credible pathway toward industrial scale.” Swiss Technology for global MarketsSonexos’ technology originated in research at EPFL and combines plasma physics, high-voltage electronics and adaptive control software. Its Plasmacoustic Metalayer™ absorbs acoustic energy directly at a surface instead of relying on conventional bulky passive absorbers or loudspeakers that cancel sound at a particular listening position.Sonexos’ initial target markets include domestic appliances, Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) and industrial systems. The company is also expanding into datacenter and energy-storage cooling, where increasingly powerful computing infrastructure is driving demand for both greater cooling capacity and effective noise management. The potential impact extends beyond acoustic performance. More compact noise-control systems can give engineers greater freedom when designing products in which space, weight and airflow are critical constraints. In applications such as data-center cooling, reducing fan noise without obstructing airflow could also help reconcile growing infrastructure needs with the interests of surrounding communities.From breakthrough technology to series production “This investment marks an important step from breakthrough technology toward industrial-scale production,” says Mark Donaldson, Founder and CEO of Sonexos. “Together with our customers and partners, we are now turning plasmacoustics into a technology that can be deployed at scale.”The investment comes at a decisive stage in Sonexos’ development. The company is already conducting paid prototype-integration programs with global manufacturers of domestic appliances and HVAC equipment. The new financing will be used primarily for industrialization, customer programs and the further development of Sonexos’ intellectual-property portfolio.The seed investment in Swiss-based Sonexos underscores Bosch Ventures’ international commitment to advancing deep-tech innovation. Complementing this international investment approach, Bosch Ventures announced its earlier this month, dedicated to investing in German deep-tech startups.

articles.title: 03.11.2026 Press release Two Wheeler EICMA 2026: Bosch is making the future of motorcycling even safer and smarter Milan, Italy – The more connected a motorcycle is, the more important it is to protect it against digital attacks. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and cloud connections are rapidly gaining importance in the two-wheeler segment. With this in mind, and with a view to protecting vehicle electronics even more effectively, Bosch is unveiling a new, highly compact generation of its Central Gateway at EICMA 2026. For Bosch, motorcycle safety has many facets. We’re making them accessible to all riders and for every vehicle class – from accident prevention through rider-assistance systems to protecting connected vehicles against external attacks,...says Geoff Liersch, head of Two-Wheeler and Powersports at Bosch. The company is introducing this new technology specifically to help motorcycle manufacturers meet upcoming regulatory requirements: starting in December 2027, in accordance with UN Regulation R155, all newly developed two-wheeled vehicles must be secured against cyberattacks as complete systems; starting in June 2029, this requirement will also apply to all new registrations.The Central Gateway serves as a central interface to control incoming data traffic. At the trade fair, Bosch is showcasing the system in two performance classes: Light and Base. The Central Gateway Light is the company’s first highly compact 16-pin version, designed for vehicles with limited installation space, which can be integrated into existing electronic architectures with minimal effort. For premium models, the 39-pin Central Gateway Base provides additional flexibility through integrated vehicle body control functions. In addition, Bosch provides its customers a high performance Central Gateway. The 99-pin Central Gateway High is designed for future generations of vehicles with highly integrated electronic architectures. Security chips built directly into the respective control units – such as the ABS or the ECU – serve as an additional layer of protection inside the vehicle. The components are designed with cybersecurity in mind right from the factory, making it easier for vehicle manufacturers to obtain type approval in accordance with international standards. They ensure that, even in the event of external access, only verified signals reach the network. In addition, Bosch offers security services throughout the vehicle’s lifecycle such as fleet monitoring, proactive attack and intrusion detection, and vulnerability tracking during operation. “With our technology, manufacturers can meet the new global requirements while protecting riders against cyberattacks on vehicle components,” explains Geoff Liersch.Bosch presents the mobility technology of tomorrowIn addition to cybersecurity, Bosch is also continuing to advance safety and convenience on the road. When it comes to Radar-based Assistance Systems (ARAS Advanced Rider Assistance Systems), Bosch is focusing on proven technologies at EICMA: with unique features, Bosch ensures safe riding in groups or in heavy traffic. The new Triumph Tiger 1200, for example, features Bosch front and rear radar sensors to increase safety and comfort, enabling a comprehensive range of Advanced Rider Assistance Systems. This integrated package combines functions such as Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), Group Ride Assist (GRA), and Riding Distance Assist (RDA) to increase safety and convenience while riding. Forward Collision Warning (FCW) and Blind Spot Detection (BSD) provide additional assistance by improving the rider’s awareness in all traffic situations.The display also plays a central role as the human-machine interface: Bosch’s TFT Connect System is a new generation of high-resolution instrument clusters that can be customized and connected to a smartphone. These can display not only important functions but also content such as navigation or music directly on the screen. In addition, the displays serve as a digital interface for activating functions at a later time (on-demand functions). The 7-inch version of the display is celebrating an important milestone at EICMA: the start of production in the new Triumph Tiger 1200 model.Turning to electrification, Bosch also offers a broad portfolio of powertrain systems. For smaller two-wheeled vehicles, the electric motor and inverter can be combined into a single integrated 6 kW electric drive, which makes integration easier for manufacturers. Compact electric in-hub motors provide emissions-free propulsion for e-scooters. Meanwhile, the Vehicle Control Unit (eVCU) is responsible for coordinating the entire electric powertrain. Another key focus is on a system solution for the Digital Battery Passport, which becomes a legal requirement in February 2027: this Bosch software provides motorcycle manufacturers with solutions for securely managing the required battery data throughout their vehicles’ lifecycle.

articles.title: 06.11.2026 Press release Mobility When every gram counts: Bosch Motorsport and the Bosch Additive Solution Center ... Abstatt, Nuremberg – From initial design concept to track-ready high-performance component in just a few weeks: Bosch Motorsport is helping racing teams, motorsport OEMs, and performance vehicle manufacturers get innovative components onto the track significantly faster. Partnering with the Bosch Additive Solution Center (ASC) in Nuremberg, Bosch Motorsport combines decades of racing engineering expertise with cutting-edge additive manufacturing to deliver highly durable metal components.Minimizing Development Time, Maximizing PerformanceBy utilizing state-of-the-art metal 3D printing technologies, Bosch Motorsport and the Nuremberg ASC drastically shorten development cycles. New component designs can be flexibly realized and tested. Because different design variations can be manufactured in parallel, their suitability can be compared quickly on the test bench or under real track conditions. These optimized iteration loops accelerate the transfer of innovative concepts directly into the vehicle, providing immediate benefits to developers and race teams.Design Freedom and Targeted LightweightingThe technological value lies in design freedom: while conventional manufacturing is limited by tooling, machining access, or manufacturing constraints, additive manufacturing enables complex geometries that were previously virtually impossible to produce. Using lattice and topology structures, material is strategically placed only where it is required to handle physical loads. This reduces component weight by more than 20 percent. At the same time, multiple individual parts can be consolidated into a single component, minimizing packaging space, assembly effort, and potential failure points in demanding racing conditions.High-End Materials for Enduring PerformanceThe material portfolio of the Nuremberg ASC proves that additively manufactured components have moved far beyond the prototyping niche. The facility processes a wide range of demanding, high-performance materials – from high-strength aluminum alloys and stainless steels to nickel-based superalloys like Inconel and other specialty alloys. The components withstand extreme mechanical loads, vibrations, and thermal spikes – conditions that define the standard in professional motorsport. Another advantage is toolless, print-on-demand manufacturing: replacement and development parts are produced exactly when needed. This saves storage costs and provides additional flexibility for race teams and vehicle developers.From Design to Finish: A Single-Source SolutionThe exceptional quality of these parts is rooted in the close collaboration between Bosch Motorsport and the Nuremberg ASC. The partnership covers the entire process chain – from “Design for Additive Manufacturing” and printing on large-scale industrial machines like the Nikon SLM NXG XII 600, to CNC post-processing and quality assurance. This provides customers with direct access to state-of-the-art 3D printing technology, combined with Bosch Motorsport's decades of racing expertise and the rigorous quality and industrialization standards of the automotive industry.Experience the Future of Lightweighting Live at PMWAt the PMW Expo in Cologne, the partners will demonstrate how additive manufacturing unlocks new possibilities for engineering, lightweight design, and track performance.When: November 11 and 12, 2026Where: Koelnmesse, Hall 10.1, Booth 2028
